question.text: Which sections of the manual are the study material for the permit and license tests?

answer.text: Sections B and C of the manual are the study material for both the learner permit test and the driver license test.

teaching.text: Both the permit test and the license test draw on Sections B and C, and the chapter sample questions are a review aid rather than the full question set. Remember: Study Sections B and C.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Sections B and C of the manual are the study material for both the learner permit test and the driver license test.

question.text: Can the manual alone teach you to drive?

answer.text: The manual by itself cannot teach you to drive; driving skill comes from a good instructor and lots of practice.

teaching.text: Reading teaches the rules; a good instructor and lots of practice teach the driving. Remember: Instructor plus practice.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The manual by itself cannot teach you to drive; driving skill comes from a good instructor and lots of practice.

question.text: How are the online practice tests organized?

answer.text: The online practice tests are grouped by topic, and the Guidelines for Driving practice test matches Chapters B-one and B-two of the manual.

teaching.text: Practice tests are grouped by topic, so a weak score points you to specific chapters. Remember: Practice tests by topic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The online practice tests are grouped by topic, and the Guidelines for Driving practice test matches Chapters B-one and B-two of the manual.

question.text: Which practice test spans four chapters of the manual?

answer.text: The Rules of the Road practice test spans four chapters (B-four, B-five, B-six and B-eight), while Traffic Signs and Signals maps to B-three alone and Alcohol, Other Drugs and Driving to B-seven.

teaching.text: Rules of the Road covers four chapters, more than any other practice test topic. Remember: Rules of the Road spans four.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The Rules of the Road practice test spans four chapters (B-four, B-five, B-six and B-eight), while Traffic Signs and Signals maps to B-three alone and Alcohol, Other Drugs and Driving to B-seven.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Rules of the Road spans four

question.text: What should you look for when you walk around the vehicle before getting in?

answer.text: Before getting in, walk around the vehicle and look for small children, pets or anything else in the way.

teaching.text: The walk-around is your chance to spot children, pets or obstacles you could not see from the seat. Remember: Look for kids and pets.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before getting in, walk around the vehicle and look for small children, pets or anything else in the way.

question.text: What else does the outside check of the vehicle cover?

answer.text: The outside check also covers the windows, lights, body damage, tire condition and any sign of fluid leaking.

teaching.text: Windows, lights, body damage, tires and leaks are all part of the outside check. Remember: Windows, lights, tires, leaks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The outside check also covers the windows, lights, body damage, tire condition and any sign of fluid leaking.

question.text: What should you do right after getting into the car?

answer.text: After getting in, put the key in the ignition, lock the doors and learn where every switch, gauge and pedal is and what it does.

teaching.text: Lock the doors and learn every switch, gauge and pedal before you set off. Remember: Key in, doors locked, learn controls.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After getting in, put the key in the ignition, lock the doors and learn where every switch, gauge and pedal is and what it does.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Key in, doors locked, learn controls

question.text: Which controls should you be able to find before you need them?

answer.text: You should know where the horn, turn signals, four-way flashers, headlight and dimmer switch, wiper and washer controls, parking brake and release, climate and defroster controls and gearshift are even before you need them.

teaching.text: Knowing where the flashers, wipers and defroster are means no searching in an emergency. Remember: Find every control first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You should know where the horn, turn signals, four-way flashers, headlight and dimmer switch, wiper and washer controls, parking brake and release, climate and defroster controls and gearshift are even before you need them.

question.text: Why should you never drive with the seat reclined?

answer.text: Never drive with the seat reclined or partly reclined, because it cuts your view and slows your reaction in an emergency.

teaching.text: An upright seat keeps your view clear and your reactions quick. Remember: Upright seat, faster reactions.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never drive with the seat reclined or partly reclined, because it cuts your view and slows your reaction in an emergency.

question.text: How should the seat be set for the pedals?

answer.text: Set the seat so the pedals are easy to reach and your foot can glide from accelerator to brake while your heel stays on the floor.

teaching.text: Your heel stays on the floor while your foot glides between the accelerator and the brake. Remember: Heel down, foot glides.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Set the seat so the pedals are easy to reach and your foot can glide from accelerator to brake while your heel stays on the floor.

question.text: How far forward should the seat or steering column go?

answer.text: Do not slide the seat so far forward, or pull the steering column out so far, that steering becomes awkward.

teaching.text: Sitting too far forward makes steering awkward. Remember: Not too close.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not slide the seat so far forward, or pull the steering column out so far, that steering becomes awkward.

question.text: What view should your seat position give you?

answer.text: Your seat position should give a clear view through the windshield, both side windows and every mirror.

teaching.text: From your seat you should see through the windshield, both side windows and every mirror. Remember: See every window and mirror.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Your seat position should give a clear view through the windshield, both side windows and every mirror.

question.text: How far from the steering wheel should your body be, and why?

answer.text: Keep your body roughly ten to twelve inches from the steering wheel whether or not the car has an air bag, so a deploying air bag strikes your chest instead of your chin or face.

teaching.text: At ten to twelve inches, a deploying air bag meets your chest rather than your face. Remember: Ten to twelve inches back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep your body roughly ten to twelve inches from the steering wheel whether or not the car has an air bag, so a deploying air bag strikes your chest instead of your chin or face.

question.text: How high should the top of the steering wheel sit?

answer.text: The top of the steering wheel should sit no higher than the tops of your shoulders.

teaching.text: Keep the top of the wheel at or below the tops of your shoulders. Remember: Wheel below shoulder tops.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The top of the steering wheel should sit no higher than the tops of your shoulders.

question.text: How high should the head restraint be, and what is it for?

answer.text: Raise the head restraint until it is level with the back of your head, because it is there to prevent whiplash when you are struck from behind.

teaching.text: Set the head restraint level with the back of your head to protect against whiplash from behind. Remember: Restraint level with head.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Raise the head restraint until it is level with the back of your head, because it is there to prevent whiplash when you are struck from behind.

question.text: When should you adjust the rearview mirrors?

answer.text: Adjust all three rearview mirrors only after the seat is set, and always before you start driving, aiming for the widest view and the smallest blind spots.

teaching.text: Set the seat first, then all three mirrors, and always before driving. Remember: Seat first, then mirrors.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Adjust all three rearview mirrors only after the seat is set, and always before you start driving, aiming for the widest view and the smallest blind spots.

question.text: How should the inside mirror be set?

answer.text: Set the inside mirror to frame the rear window, turned so that only the edge of the right rear window post shows.

teaching.text: The inside mirror frames the rear window, with just the edge of the right rear post showing. Remember: Frame the rear window.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Set the inside mirror to frame the rear window, turned so that only the edge of the right rear window post shows.

question.text: How do you set the left outside mirror?

answer.text: For the left mirror, rest your head against the driver's window and set the mirror until the side of your car just barely shows at its inner edge.

teaching.text: For the left mirror, lean against the driver's window and stop when your car barely shows. Remember: Head on window, sliver of car.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For the left mirror, rest your head against the driver's window and set the mirror until the side of your car just barely shows at its inner edge.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Head on window, sliver of car

question.text: How do you set the right outside mirror?

answer.text: For the right mirror, hold your head just above the center console and set it until the side of your car just barely shows at its inner edge.

teaching.text: For the right mirror, hold your head over the center console and stop when your car barely shows. Remember: Head over console, sliver.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For the right mirror, hold your head just above the center console and set it until the side of your car just barely shows at its inner edge.

question.text: How can you check that your mirrors are set well?

answer.text: To check the mirrors, let a car pass on your left: as it leaves the inside mirror, its front bumper should appear in the left outside mirror.

teaching.text: A passing car should move straight from the inside mirror into the left mirror. Remember: Bumper appears as car leaves.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To check the mirrors, let a car pass on your left: as it leaves the inside mirror, its front bumper should appear in the left outside mirror.

question.text: What should you do if you see your car's rear corners in the outside mirrors?

answer.text: If leaning back a little still shows you more than a glimpse of your car's rear corners in the outside mirrors, turn those mirrors outward.

teaching.text: If you see your car's rear corners, turn the outside mirrors outward. Remember: Corners showing, turn outward.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If leaning back a little still shows you more than a glimpse of your car's rear corners in the outside mirrors, turn those mirrors outward.

question.text: What may you need to set the passenger mirror without remote controls?

answer.text: A car without remote mirror controls may need a helper to set the passenger-side mirror correctly.

teaching.text: Without remote controls, a helper can set the passenger mirror. Remember: A helper sets it.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A car without remote mirror controls may need a helper to set the passenger-side mirror correctly.

question.text: Where should you try out new mirror settings?

answer.text: Try new mirror settings while parked, for example along a street watching passing cars, before driving into traffic with them.

teaching.text: Try new mirror settings while parked before trusting them in traffic. Remember: Test settings while parked.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Try new mirror settings while parked, for example along a street watching passing cars, before driving into traffic with them.

question.text: Do well-adjusted mirrors remove every blind spot?

answer.text: Even perfectly adjusted mirrors leave some blind spots, so always turn your head to check before turning or changing lanes.

teaching.text: No mirror setting removes every blind spot, so a head check is always needed. Remember: Always turn your head.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Even perfectly adjusted mirrors leave some blind spots, so always turn your head to check before turning or changing lanes.

question.text: How should the lap and shoulder belts be worn before driving?

answer.text: Wear the lap belt snug across your hips and the shoulder belt snug across your shoulder, and make sure every passenger is belted or in a child restraint before you drive.

teaching.text: Snug at the hips and across the shoulder, and every passenger secured before you move. Remember: Snug lap, snug shoulder.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Wear the lap belt snug across your hips and the shoulder belt snug across your shoulder, and make sure every passenger is belted or in a child restraint before you drive.

question.text: What can happen if you fail to belt yourself or secure passengers?

answer.text: Failing to belt yourself or to secure passengers in a car seat or booster seat can bring a fine, and the passenger-protection chapter covers the full rules.

teaching.text: An unbelted driver or unsecured passenger can mean a fine. Remember: Unbelted means a fine.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Failing to belt yourself or to secure passengers in a car seat or booster seat can bring a fine, and the passenger-protection chapter covers the full rules.

question.text: How do you start most automatic and manual cars?

answer.text: To start most cars, keep your foot on the brake with an automatic in PARK or a manual in NEUTRAL; a manual car needs the parking brake set and the clutch pressed before it will start.

teaching.text: Foot on the brake every time; a manual also needs the parking brake set and the clutch pressed. Remember: Brake down, then start.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To start most cars, keep your foot on the brake with an automatic in PARK or a manual in NEUTRAL; a manual car needs the parking brake set and the clutch pressed before it will start.

question.text: What should you check when the key is turned to on?

answer.text: With the key turned to on, check the dashboard lights and gauges, such as the antilock brake, air bag and fuel indicators, for warnings.

teaching.text: Turning the key to on is the moment to scan for warning lights. Remember: Scan the warning lights.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With the key turned to on, check the dashboard lights and gauges, such as the antilock brake, air bag and fuel indicators, for warnings.

question.text: When should you use low-beam headlights, and what do they do in daylight?

answer.text: Use low-beam headlights especially at night or in bad weather; even in normal daylight, headlights make a vehicle visible from twice as far away.

teaching.text: Headlights double the distance from which others can see you, even in daylight. Remember: Lights on, seen sooner.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use low-beam headlights especially at night or in bad weather; even in normal daylight, headlights make a vehicle visible from twice as far away.

question.text: What do R, D and O mean in an automatic car?

answer.text: In an automatic car, R is reverse and D is drive, and some newer cars add an O overdrive setting meant for interstates with little stop-and-go traffic.

teaching.text: Overdrive is for interstates with little stop-and-go traffic. Remember: Reverse, drive, overdrive.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In an automatic car, R is reverse and D is drive, and some newer cars add an O overdrive setting meant for interstates with little stop-and-go traffic.

question.text: What are the lower gears in an automatic used for?

answer.text: The lower gears marked L, two or one are for special cases such as steep mountain descents, slow driving on ice or slippery roads, and slowing down if the brakes fail.

teaching.text: The low gears are for steep descents, slippery roads and brake failure. Remember: Low gears for special cases.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The lower gears marked L, two or one are for special cases such as steep mountain descents, slow driving on ice or slippery roads, and slowing down if the brakes fail.

question.text: How can a manual transmission help slow the car?

answer.text: A manual transmission lets the driver use gears instead of brakes to help slow the car, and you should shift to a lower gear going down steep hills.

teaching.text: In a manual car, a lower gear helps slow you down a steep hill. Remember: Downshift on steep hills.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A manual transmission lets the driver use gears instead of brakes to help slow the car, and you should shift to a lower gear going down steep hills.

question.text: When must you push the clutch all the way down?

answer.text: With a manual transmission, push the clutch all the way down when starting, when shifting and once your speed falls below ten miles per hour while stopping.

teaching.text: Press the clutch fully when starting, when shifting and when slowing below ten miles per hour. Remember: Clutch down to start, shift, stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With a manual transmission, push the clutch all the way down when starting, when shifting and once your speed falls below ten miles per hour while stopping.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Clutch down to start, shift, stop

question.text: What clutch and neutral habits are not allowed?

answer.text: Coasting with the gears in neutral is illegal, and you should not rest your foot on the clutch when you are not changing gears.

teaching.text: Coasting in neutral is illegal, and riding the clutch between shifts is a habit to avoid. Remember: Never coast in neutral.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Coasting with the gears in neutral is illegal, and you should not rest your foot on the clutch when you are not changing gears.

question.text: Why should you never turn the ignition to lock while moving?

answer.text: In a car with a steering wheel interlock, never turn the ignition to lock while moving, because the wheel will lock and you will lose control.

teaching.text: Turning to lock while moving freezes the steering wheel in an interlock car. Remember: Lock means lost steering.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a car with a steering wheel interlock, never turn the ignition to lock while moving, because the wheel will lock and you will lose control.

question.text: How should you hold the steering wheel?

answer.text: Keep both hands on the wheel with a relaxed but firm grip, and do not prop your elbow on the door or hang your arm out the window.

teaching.text: Both hands, relaxed but firm, with no elbow on the door. Remember: Both hands, firm grip.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep both hands on the wheel with a relaxed but firm grip, and do not prop your elbow on the door or hang your arm out the window.

question.text: How should your arms be positioned at the wheel?

answer.text: Your elbows should bend slightly when your palm reaches the top of the wheel, and you should never sit with your arms locked straight.

teaching.text: Bend your elbows slightly; never lock your arms straight. Remember: Elbows slightly bent.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Your elbows should bend slightly when your palm reaches the top of the wheel, and you should never sit with your arms locked straight.

question.text: When does your hand position change briefly?

answer.text: Your hand position will change briefly while you work the turn signal, headlight dimmer or wiper controls.

teaching.text: Your hands leave nine and three only briefly to work the controls. Remember: Hands move for controls.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Your hand position will change briefly while you work the turn signal, headlight dimmer or wiper controls.

question.text: Why should your arm not rest on the door or out the window?

answer.text: An arm resting on the door or out the window gives you less control of the wheel and could be severed in a sideswipe.

teaching.text: An arm on the door or out the window means less control and real injury risk in a sideswipe. Remember: Arms inside the car.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: An arm resting on the door or out the window gives you less control of the wheel and could be severed in a sideswipe.

question.text: What part do your eyes play in steering?

answer.text: You steer with your eyes as well as your hands: look where you want to go, and let your side vision help hold your lane position.

teaching.text: Your eyes guide the car: look where you want to go. Remember: Look where you go.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You steer with your eyes as well as your hands: look where you want to go, and let your side vision help hold your lane position.

question.text: Where should your hands sit on the steering wheel?

answer.text: Picture the wheel as a clock and put your left hand at nine o'clock and your right at three o'clock, a position that helps avoid air bag injuries.

teaching.text: Nine and three keeps your hands out of harm's way if the air bag deploys. Remember: Nine and three.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Picture the wheel as a clock and put your left hand at nine o'clock and your right at three o'clock, a position that helps avoid air bag injuries.

question.text: How should you bring the wheel back after a turn?

answer.text: Coming out of a turn, reverse the hand movements instead of letting the wheel slide through your fingers; this counter-steering also helps in skids and on snow and ice.

teaching.text: Reverse your hands to straighten out instead of letting the wheel slide through your fingers. Remember: Reverse hands, no sliding.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Coming out of a turn, reverse the hand movements instead of letting the wheel slide through your fingers; this counter-steering also helps in skids and on snow and ice.

question.text: Is crossing your wrists or your arms acceptable while turning?

answer.text: Crossing your wrists during a turn is fine, but crossing your arms is not, because clothing or jewelry can snag and an air bag would injure you more.

teaching.text: Wrists may cross on a turn, but arms should not. Remember: Wrists may cross, arms never.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Crossing your wrists during a turn is fine, but crossing your arms is not, because clothing or jewelry can snag and an air bag would injure you more.

question.text: Which steering method is recommended, and why?

answer.text: The push-pull method is the recommended way to steer because it slows the turn and keeps both hands on the wheel the whole time.

teaching.text: Push-pull keeps both hands on the wheel and slows the turn. Remember: Push-pull keeps both hands.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The push-pull method is the recommended way to steer because it slows the turn and keeps both hands on the wheel the whole time.

question.text: What are the clock positions in a push-pull left turn?

answer.text: In a push-pull left turn the left hand pulls down to about seven o'clock while the right pushes up to about one o'clock; a right turn mirrors this, with the right hand pulling to about five and the left pushing to about eleven.

teaching.text: For a left turn, the left hand pulls to seven while the right hand pushes to one. Remember: Pull to seven, push to one.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a push-pull left turn the left hand pulls down to about seven o'clock while the right pushes up to about one o'clock; a right turn mirrors this, with the right hand pulling to about five and the left pushing to about eleven.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Pull to seven, push to one

question.text: What is the risk of hand-over-hand steering?

answer.text: Hand-over-hand steering turns the wheel faster but crosses the hands at the top and sometimes leaves only one hand on the wheel, so keep your speed down when using it.

teaching.text: Hand-over-hand is quicker but can leave one hand on the wheel, so keep the speed down. Remember: Faster turn, keep slow.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hand-over-hand steering turns the wheel faster but crosses the hands at the top and sometimes leaves only one hand on the wheel, so keep your speed down when using it.

question.text: How do you make a hand-over-hand right turn?

answer.text: For a hand-over-hand right turn, reach forward to grip the rim at one o'clock palm down, pull to five o'clock, repeat with the other hand, and return to nine and three before counter-steering out.

teaching.text: In a hand-over-hand right turn, each hand grips at one and pulls to five in turn. Remember: Grip at one, pull to five.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For a hand-over-hand right turn, reach forward to grip the rim at one o'clock palm down, pull to five o'clock, repeat with the other hand, and return to nine and three before counter-steering out.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Grip at one, pull to five

question.text: What mistakes do new drivers make most often when backing?

answer.text: New drivers backing up most often go too fast, steer too much or turn the wheel the wrong way.

teaching.text: Speed, oversteering and turning the wrong way are the classic backing errors. Remember: Too fast, too much.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: New drivers backing up most often go too fast, steer too much or turn the wheel the wrong way.

question.text: How should you position yourself to back up?

answer.text: To back up, hold the wheel at twelve o'clock with your left hand, put your right arm over the seat back and look through the rear window, turning the wheel toward the side you want to move to.

teaching.text: Left hand at twelve, right arm over the seat, eyes out the rear window. Remember: Left hand high, look back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To back up, hold the wheel at twelve o'clock with your left hand, put your right arm over the seat back and look through the rear window, turning the wheel toward the side you want to move to.

question.text: How fast should you go while backing, and where should you look?

answer.text: While backing, keep to idle speed or gentle acceleration and keep looking to the rear until the car has fully stopped.

teaching.text: Back at idle speed and keep looking back until you have fully stopped. Remember: Idle slow, eyes back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: While backing, keep to idle speed or gentle acceleration and keep looking to the rear until the car has fully stopped.

question.text: Where should you look when pulling away?

answer.text: When pulling away, look at least one block ahead and steer toward a reference point.

teaching.text: Looking a block ahead helps you pull away straight and steady. Remember: A block ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When pulling away, look at least one block ahead and steer toward a reference point.

question.text: What should you check before pulling forward?

answer.text: Before pulling forward, check ahead, to the sides and behind, signal if leaving a curb, then move your foot to the accelerator and press gently.

teaching.text: Check all around, signal from a curb, then press the accelerator gently. Remember: Check around, signal, ease on.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before pulling forward, check ahead, to the sides and behind, signal if leaving a curb, then move your foot to the accelerator and press gently.

question.text: What is Tennessee's most common type of crash each year?

answer.text: Tennessee reports rear-end collisions as the most common type of crash each year, which is why smooth, planned stops matter.

teaching.text: Since rear-end crashes are the most common in Tennessee, plan every stop. Remember: Rear-end is most common.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Tennessee reports rear-end collisions as the most common type of crash each year, which is why smooth, planned stops matter.

question.text: How do you make a smooth stop?

answer.text: For a smooth stop, check your mirrors, ease off the accelerator, move your foot to the brake and press with steady pressure rather than stomping.

teaching.text: Mirrors, ease off, then steady brake pressure: no stomping. Remember: Mirrors, ease off, steady.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For a smooth stop, check your mirrors, ease off the accelerator, move your foot to the brake and press with steady pressure rather than stomping.

question.text: Where should you stop at a stop sign or signal?

answer.text: At a stop sign or signal, stop before the crosswalk or marked stop line; if there is neither, stop where you can see traffic on the cross road before entering the intersection.

teaching.text: Stop before the line or crosswalk, or where you can see cross traffic if there is neither. Remember: Stop before the line.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a stop sign or signal, stop before the crosswalk or marked stop line; if there is neither, stop where you can see traffic on the cross road before entering the intersection.

question.text: How close to the curb should you park?

answer.text: When parking at a curb, pull within eighteen inches of it.

teaching.text: Eighteen inches from the curb is the closest guide for parking. Remember: Within eighteen inches.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When parking at a curb, pull within eighteen inches of it.

question.text: What is the safest habit once you are a competent driver?

answer.text: Once you become a competent driver, the safest habit is not letting your attention to driving slip.

teaching.text: Staying attentive is the habit that keeps a competent driver safe. Remember: Stay attentive always.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Once you become a competent driver, the safest habit is not letting your attention to driving slip.

question.text: Why is carbon monoxide so dangerous, and where does it come from?

answer.text: Carbon monoxide from the engine can kill and cannot be tasted, smelled or seen; it tends to leak while the heater runs, when the exhaust system is faulty, or from other cars' fumes in heavy traffic.

teaching.text: You cannot taste, smell or see carbon monoxide, so prevention is the only defense. Remember: Invisible, odorless, deadly.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Carbon monoxide from the engine can kill and cannot be tasted, smelled or seen; it tends to leak while the heater runs, when the exhaust system is faulty, or from other cars' fumes in heavy traffic.

question.text: Where should you never run the engine or the heater?

answer.text: Never run the engine in a closed garage, and never use the heater or air conditioner in a parked car with the windows shut.

teaching.text: A closed garage or a sealed parked car lets carbon monoxide build up. Remember: No engine in closed garage.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never run the engine in a closed garage, and never use the heater or air conditioner in a parked car with the windows shut.

question.text: How can you guard against carbon monoxide?

answer.text: To guard against carbon monoxide, have the exhaust checked regularly, listen for unusual roaring under the car and close the fresh-air vent in heavy traffic.

teaching.text: Regular exhaust checks and a closed vent in heavy traffic help keep carbon monoxide out. Remember: Check exhaust, close vent.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To guard against carbon monoxide, have the exhaust checked regularly, listen for unusual roaring under the car and close the fresh-air vent in heavy traffic.

question.text: What does the Hands Free Tennessee law forbid?

answer.text: Under the Hands Free Tennessee law, a driver may not hold a phone or mobile device with any part of the body or write, send or read any text-based message.

teaching.text: The hands-free law bans holding the device and handling text messages while driving. Remember: Hands off the phone.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Under the Hands Free Tennessee law, a driver may not hold a phone or mobile device with any part of the body or write, send or read any text-based message.

question.text: What else does the hands-free law forbid besides holding a device?

answer.text: The hands-free law also forbids reaching for a device in a way that takes you out of your seated, belted position, and watching, recording or broadcasting video on it.

teaching.text: The law also bars reaching out of your belted position for a device and using video on it. Remember: No reaching, no video.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The hands-free law also forbids reaching for a device in a way that takes you out of your seated, belted position, and watching, recording or broadcasting video on it.

question.text: What did the older two thousand nine phone rule ban?
